findings.title: BlockedEmail.should_block? has a lost-update race condition
findings.body: should_block? performs a non-atomic read-modify-write: it loads the record via `where(email: email).first`, increments match_count in Ruby memory, and saves. Under two concurrent requests for the same blocked email, both callers can read the same match_count, both increment it to N+1, and both write back, losing one increment. The persisted match_count will be smaller than the actual number of attempts, and last_match_at will lag behind the true last occurrence. The increment must be atomic (e.g., `record.increment!(:match_count)` plus `update_column(:last_match_at, Time.zone.now)`, or a single SQL UPDATE statement), and ideally wrapped in a single statement that does not depend on a previously read row.

findings.title: EmailValidator triggers DB writes on every validation via BlockedEmail.should_block?
findings.body: validate_each calls BlockedEmail.should_block?, which writes to the blocked_emails table (match_count and last_match_at) on every match. ActiveRecord typically runs validators multiple times during a single save: the controller calls `user.valid?` before save, ActiveRecord re-runs validations inside save, and re-runs them again on retries after uniqueness/format errors. Each blocked-email signup therefore inflates match_count several times and adds several UPDATE queries to the request path. Worse, calling `record.valid?` (without saving) still updates persisted state, which is surprising for a validator. Statistics tracking should be moved out of the validator (e.g., to an after_validation hook on User, or a Redis counter incremented only on actual save) so validation remains side-effect free and counters are not inflated.

findings.title: BlockedEmail lookup is case-sensitive, allowing blocklist bypass via email casing
findings.body: `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` is a case-sensitive comparison, so a blocklist row stored as `bad@spamclub.com` will not match `BAD@spamclub.com`, `Bad@spamclub.com`, or any other case variant. This is inconsistent with the rest of the user-facing email code: User.find_by_username_or_email calls Email.downcase before lookup, the regex built in EmailValidator#email_in_restriction_setting? matches regardless of case, and email comparisons elsewhere in the codebase are case-insensitive. An attacker registering with a case-variant email bypasses the block entirely. The lookup should normalize (e.g., `BlockedEmail.where(email: email.downcase).first`) or emails should be lowercased on insert (with a citext/case-insensitive column), and the matching test should explicitly assert case-variant behavior.

findings.title: EmailValidator whitelist/blacklist logic is not covered by tests
findings.body: The original User#email_validator implemented two branches (SiteSetting.email_domains_whitelist and SiteSetting.email_domains_blacklist) that were extracted into lib/validators/email_validator.rb. The new spec only stubs BlockedEmail.should_block? and never sets email_domains_whitelist or email_domains_blacklist, so the regex-based domain matching, the priority between the whitelist and the blacklist (if/elsif), and the email_in_restriction_setting? helper are completely untested. The .gsub('.', '\.') escaping, the @-anchored regex, and the if/elsif precedence are non-trivial and easy to silently regress, so each branch (whitelist match, whitelist mismatch, blacklist match, blacklist mismatch, both unset) needs at least one explicit test.
